verses.text: Then I returned and saw all the oppressions that are done under the sun: and behold, the tears of those who were oppressed, and they had no comforter; and on the side of their oppressors there was power; but they had no comforter.
Therefore I praised the dead who have been long dead more than the living who are yet alive.
Yes, better than them both is him who has not yet been, who has not seen the evil work that is done under the sun.
Then I saw all the labor and achievement that is the envy of a man’s neighbor. This also is vanity and a striving after wind.
The fool folds his hands together and ruins himself.
Better is a handful, with quietness, than two handfuls with labor and chasing after wind.
Then I returned and saw vanity under the sun.

There is one who is alone, and he has neither son nor brother. There is no end to all of his labor, neither are his eyes satisfied with wealth. “For whom then, do I labor, and deprive my soul of enjoyment?” This also is vanity. Yes, it is a miserable business.
Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
Better is a poor and wise youth than an old and foolish king who doesn’t know how to receive admonition any more.
For out of prison he came out to be king; yes, even in his kingdom he was born poor.
I saw all the living who walk under the sun, that they were with the youth, the other, who succeeded him.
There was no end of all the people, even of all them over whom he was — yet those who come after shall not rejoice in him. Surely this also is vanity and a chasing after wind.

footnotes.content: The Teacher sees cruelty plainly—tears without comfort, oppressors holding power unchecked. I've learned that God's eye marks every sorrow the world tries to ignore. He sees not just the injustice, but the lonely pain beside it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When the Teacher praises the dead over the living, he's not wishing death on anyone—he's saying there's a rest in finishing well that the still-living can't yet know. I've watched weary souls find a strange peace in that promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Better still, says the Teacher, is one who never arrives at all—never sees the brokenness firsthand. Yet Jesus came anyway, saw it all, and still loved us into redemption. That willingness breaks my heart every time.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Work that springs from envy—wanting what your neighbor has—is just grasping at wind. The Teacher names a poison I've seen cripple many. Jesus teaches us to labor with open hands, letting Him define what's enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fool won't lift a finger; idleness eats from within. Yet the opposite—frantic striving—is just as ruinous. God calls us to diligent work done in peace, trusting His provision. That's the narrow way.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A quiet handful beats fistfuls gained through exhaustion. I've known people rich in peace and poor in rest—and poor in soul despite their wealth. The Teacher teaches us to measure twice here: What am I actually keeping?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Teacher turns to contemplate emptiness again. This returns us to the big questions: Is it all hollow? I've found it isn't—not if we rest our work in Christ and serve others, not ourselves.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A person alone, working endlessly, never satisfied—never asking 'For whom?' That hollow question reveals the tragedy: we're made for connection, for love, for someone beyond ourselves. God built that longing into us on purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Two are better than one—this truth runs deep. In company, work bears good fruit; in solitude, it withers. God placed us in community. A burden shared halves the weight; a joy shared doubles the light.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: When one falls, the other lifts them. The Teacher sketches loneliness like a wound—falling with no one to help. I think of Jesus sending disciples two by two, never one alone. He knew we need a hand when we stumble.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Warmth shared—a simple image of belonging. In the cold night, we need each other's presence. The gospel speaks this way too: gathered together in His name, there's a warmth no solitude can touch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One falls easily; two push back. Three cords twisted hold strong. The Teacher celebrates the power of unity—not for conquest, but for standing firm together. In faith, we're never truly alone against the night.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A wise youth beats a foolish king who won't take instruction. Wisdom is teachable; it stays humble and open. Jesus taught and was himself the greatest teacher—His kingdom values the lowly learner above the proud ruler.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From prison to throne—grace writes a long arc. Yet the Teacher sees even that rise as empty if the person stays stubborn. True rule is service. Jesus washed feet and called us to do the same.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: People gather around the wise youth, the successor. Power draws crowds for a moment. I've watched kingdoms rise and shift their allegiance at the next wind. Only Jesus holds hearts forever—not by force, but by love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse: the endless succession, the forgotten ruler, the hollow triumph. Yet we know someone whose name is never forgotten, whose kingdom doesn't fade when He leaves the throne—because He never leaves us. That's the hope the Teacher points toward without quite naming it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
